claim: Plasmodium falciparum causes malaria in humans with over 450,000 deaths annually.
source: Plasmodium falciparum causes malaria in humans with over 450,000 deaths annually.
evidence: This is a statement of epidemiological fact presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The asexual blood stage of P. falciparum involves invasion of erythrocytes by merozoites.
source: The asexual blood stage involves invasion of erythrocytes by merozoites, in which they grow and divide to release daughter merozoites, which in turn invade new erythrocytes perpetuating the cycle responsible for malaria.
evidence: This describes the established life cycle of the parasite, representing general knowledge in malaria biology.

claim: A key step in merozoite invasion is the essential binding of PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex to basigin.
source: A key step in merozoite invasion is the essential binding of PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex to basigin, a step linked to the formation of a pore between merozoites and erythrocytes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the field, as indicated in the introduction section.

claim: CyRPA interacts directly with PfRh5.
source: We show CyRPA interacts directly with PfRh5.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C demonstrating complex formation by SEC and co-immunoprecipitation.

claim: An invasion inhibitory monoclonal antibody to CyRPA blocks binding of CyRPA to PfRh5.
source: An invasion inhibitory monoclonal antibody to CyRPA blocks binding of CyRPA to PfRh5 and complex formation thus illuminating the molecular mechanism for inhibition of parasite growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating that antibody 8A7 prevents complex formation.

claim: CyRPA has a six-bladed β-propeller fold.
source: CyRPA has a six-bladed β-propeller fold, and we identify the region that interacts with PfRh5.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure determination described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The functionally conserved epitope on CyRPA is a potential target for vaccines against P. falciparum.
source: This functionally conserved epitope is a potential target for vaccines against P. falciparum.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the structural and functional data presented, suggesting future applications.

claim: There are approximately 214 million malaria cases each year.
source: The most severe form of malaria in humans is caused by P. falciparum with approximately 214 million cases and over 450,000 deaths each year occurring mostly in subtropical and tropical regions of the world (Who, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from a WHO report (Who, 2015).

claim: Infection of humans by P. falciparum occurs during blood feeding by a female Anopheles mosquito.
source: Infection of humans occurs during blood feeding by a female Anopheles mosquito.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about malaria transmission.

claim: After development in hepatocytes, liver merozoites are released that quickly invade erythrocytes in the circulating blood.
source: The injected parasites migrate to the liver, and after development in hepatocytes liver merozoites are released that quickly invade erythrocytes in the circulating blood.
evidence: This describes the established life cycle of the malaria parasite.

claim: The parasites grow and divide to produce 16 to 32 new daughter merozoites.
source: The parasites grow and divide to produce 16 to 32 new daughter merozoites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the asexual replication cycle of P. falciparum.

claim: Invasion of human erythrocytes by P. falciparum merozoites involves multiple interactions of ligands with host receptors in a complex multistep process.
source: Invasion of human erythrocytes by P. falciparum merozoites involves multiple interactions of ligands with host receptors in a complex multistep process that ultimately ends with the internalization of the parasite (reviewed in [Cowman and Crabb, 2006]).
evidence: This is supported by a review citation (Cowman and Crabb, 2006).

claim: The initial interaction of the parasite with the erythrocyte membrane is driven by low affinity interactions involving surface proteins that facilitate apical reorientation.
source: The initial interaction of the parasite with the erythrocyte membrane is driven by low affinity interactions involving surface proteins that facilitate apical reorientation.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the invasion process.

claim: PfRh5 is a disparate member of the PfRh family of ligands because it is small and lacks a transmembrane domain.
source: PfRh5 is a disparate member of the PfRh family of ligands because, unlike other members of this protein family, it is small and lacks a transmembrane domain (Hayton et al., 2008; Baum et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Hayton et al., 2008; Baum et al., 2009).

claim: PfRh5 binds to basigin on the erythrocyte surface.
source: PfRh5 binds to basigin on the erythrocyte surface (Crosnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Crosnier et al., 2011.

claim: The crystal structures of PfRh5 alone and in complex with its receptor basigin have been determined.
source: The crystal structures of PfRh5 alone (Chen et al., 2014) and in complex with its receptor basigin (Wright et al., 2014) have been determined and the Rh domain shown to exhibit a novel fold.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies (Chen et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2014).

claim: PfRh5 forms a complex with CyRPA and PfRipr.
source: PfRh5 forms a complex with cysteine-rich protective antigen (CyRPA) and P. falciparum Rh5 interacting protein (PfRipr) (Chen et al., 2011a; Reddy et al., 2015; Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Chen et al., 2011a; Reddy et al., 2015; Volz et al., 2016).

claim: The function of PfRh5 is essential.
source: The function of PfRh5 is essential and blocking of its interaction with basigin using either soluble basigin or specific antibodies inhibits merozoite invasion (Volz et al., 2016; Weiss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Volz et al., 2016; Weiss et al., 2015).

claim: P. falciparum merozoites in which the cyrpa or pfripr genes have been conditionally disrupted cannot invade human erythrocytes.
source: Furthermore, P. falciparum merozoites in which the cyrpa or pfripr genes have been conditionally disrupted also cannot invade human erythrocytes and this process is blocked at the same point as observed when PfRh5 function is inhibited (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Volz et al., 2016.

claim: The function of the PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex has been associated with the formation of a discontinuity or pore between the merozoite and the erythrocyte that allows movement of Ca2+ into the host cell.
source: The function of the PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex has been associated with the formation of a discontinuity or pore between the merozoite and the erythrocyte that allows movement of Ca2+ into the host cell.
evidence: This is based on prior work cited in the manuscript (Volz et al., 2016; Weiss et al., 2015).

claim: CyRPA and PfRipr are localized in the micronemes.
source: CyRPA and PfRipr are localized in the micronemes whereas PfRh5 is present at the neck of the rhoptries and these proteins are released onto the surface during merozoite invasion (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Volz et al., 2016.

claim: PfRh5 is present at the neck of the rhoptries.
source: CyRPA and PfRipr are localized in the micronemes whereas PfRh5 is present at the neck of the rhoptries and these proteins are released onto the surface during merozoite invasion (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Volz et al., 2016.

claim: The tripartite complex forms only at the interface between the invading parasite membrane and the erythrocyte membrane.
source: Super-resolution microscopy has shown that the tripartite complex forms only at the interface between the invading parasite membrane and the erythrocyte membrane, with pools of PfRh5, CyRPA and PfRipr spread over the surface of the merozoite (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Volz et al., 2016.

claim: CyRPA does not have a GPI anchor.
source: However, it was subsequently shown that CyRPA does not have a GPI anchor, and, as none of these proteins have a transmembrane domain, it remains unclear how they associate with the parasite's plasma membrane (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Volz et al., 2016.

claim: Antibodies to PfRh5, PfRipr and CyRPA inhibit merozoite invasion.
source: Antibodies to PfRh5, PfRipr and CyRPA inhibit merozoite invasion and these proteins are important blood stage malaria vaccine candidates (Chen et al., 2011a; Douglas et al., 2011; Williams et al., 2012; Patel et al., 2013; Reddy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Chen et al., 2011a; Douglas et al., 2011; Williams et al., 2012; Patel et al., 2013; Reddy et al., 2014).

claim: CyRPA-specific monoclonal antibodies inhibit growth of P. falciparum in NOD-scid IL2Rynull mice engrafted with human erythrocytes.
source: CyRPA-specific monoclonal antibodies inhibit growth of P. falciparum in a NOD-scid IL2Rynull mice engrafted with human erythrocytes (Dreyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dreyer et al., 2012.

claim: A PfRh5-based vaccine has been shown to be efficacious in P. falciparum challenged aotus monkeys.
source: Additionally, a PfRh5-based vaccine has been shown to be efficacious in P. falciparum challenged aotus monkeys (Douglas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Douglas et al., 2015.

claim: The crystal structure of CyRPA in complex with Fab fragment was determined using diffraction data to 2.44 Å resolution.
source: We have determined the crystal structure of this complex using diffraction data to 2.44 Å resolution and shown that CyRPA has a six-bladed β-propeller fold.
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: The structure of uncomplexed CyRPA was determined using data to 3.09 Å resolution.
source: We have also determined the structure of the uncomplexed CyRPA using data to 3.09 Å resolution.
evidence: This is supported by the crystallographic data presented in Table 1.

claim: Full-length mature CyRPA was expressed in insect cells and purified to homogeneity.
source: Full-length mature CyRPA (residues 30–362 of the translated protein product) was expressed in insect cells and purified to homogeneity as evidenced by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) and SDS-PAGE analysis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Recombinant CyRPA can bind to PfRh5 to form a stable 1:1 complex.
source: To determine if the recombinant CyRPA can bind to PfRh5 (Chen et al., 2014), we combined the two proteins and showed by SEC they are capable of forming a stable 1:1 complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CyRPA co-precipitated with FLAG-tagged PfRh5 in immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: CyRPA/PfRh5 complex formation was also confirmed by incubation of excess CyRPA with FLAG-tagged PfRh5 followed by immunoprecipitation with anti-FLAG antibodies. In these experiments, CyRPA co-precipitated with PfRh5 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The recombinant CyRPA is correctly folded and functionally competent.
source: These experiments also indicate that our recombinant CyRPA is correctly folded and also functionally competent.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of recombinant CyRPA to bind PfRh5 as shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Three monoclonal antibodies (5B12, 3D1 and 8A7) inhibited P. falciparum growth to approximately 70% at 2 mg/ml.
source: Three monoclonal antibodies (5B12, 3D1 and 8A7) were identified that inhibited growth to approximately 70% at 2 mg/ml, whereas others (7A6 and 8B9) showed essentially no inhibition (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Monoclonal antibodies 7A6 and 8B9 showed essentially no inhibition of P. falciparum growth.
source: Three monoclonal antibodies (5B12, 3D1 and 8A7) were identified that inhibited growth to approximately 70% at 2 mg/ml, whereas others (7A6 and 8B9) showed essentially no inhibition (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Antibodies that blocked parasite growth reacted with a conformational epitope as they bound to non-reduced protein but not to reduced protein.
source: Immunoblot analysis of CyRPA with the monoclonal antibodies showed those that blocked parasite growth reacted with a conformational epitope as they bound to non-reduced protein but not to reduced protein (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Antibodies that did not inhibit parasite growth reacted with both reduced and non-reduced CyRPA, consistent with them binding to a linear epitope.
source: In contrast, the antibodies that did not inhibit parasite growth reacted with both reduced and non-reduced CyRPA, consistent with them binding to a linear epitope.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The three inhibitory anti-CyRPA monoclonal antibodies (5B12, 3D1 and 8A7) have a similar potency as the inhibitory anti-Ripr monoclonal antibody 5G6 in growth inhibition assays.
source: The three inhibitory anti-CyRPA monoclonal antibodies (5B12, 3D1 and 8A7) have a similar potency as the inhibitory anti-Ripr monoclonal antibody 5G6 in the growth inhibition assays (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Monoclonal antibody 8A7 blocked binding of PfRh5 to CyRPA.
source: Monoclonal antibody 8A7 blocked binding of PfRh5 to CyRPA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the presence of inhibitory monoclonal antibody 8A7, the formation of the PfRh5/CyRPA complex is disrupted with PfRh5 eluted alone in the later fractions.
source: In the presence of inhibitory monoclonal antibody 8A7, the formation of the PfRh5/CyRPA complex is disrupted with PfRh5 eluted alone in the later fractions (Figure 2C), and CyRPA eluted as a complex with 8A7 in the earlier fractions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the presence of non-inhibitory monoclonal antibody 7A6, CyRPA remains bound to PfRh5.
source: However, in the presence of non-inhibitory monoclonal antibody 7A6, CyRPA remains bound to PfRh5 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The antibody 7A6 did not bind to native CyRPA consistent with binding to a linear epitope that is not exposed on the surface of the protein.
source: The antibody 7A6 also did not bind to native CyRPA consistent with binding to a linear epitope in immunoblots (Figure 2B) that is not exposed on the surface of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: In the presence of non-inhibitory anti-PfRh5 monoclonal antibody 4G4, the PfRh5/CyRPA complex remained largely intact and was eluted as a tri-molecular complex in the earlier fractions.
source: In addition, in the presence of non-inhibitory anti-PfRh5 monoclonal antibody 4G4 (Figure 2A), the PfRh5/CyRPA complex remained largely intact and was eluted as a tri-molecular complex in the earlier fractions, with free CyRPA eluted in the later fractions (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The growth-inhibitory mechanism of the monoclonal antibody 8A7 is likely due to the disruption of PfRh5/CyRPA complex formation.
source: These results suggested that growth-inhibitory mechanism of the monoclonal antibody 8A7 is likely due to the disruption of PfRh5/CyRPA complex formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that 8A7 blocks complex formation (Figure 2C).

claim: The structure of the CyRPA/Fab complex was determined by molecular replacement using a homologous Fab fragment to obtain initial phases.
source: The structure of the complex was determined using diffraction data to 2.44 Å resolution by molecular replacement using a homologous Fab fragment to obtain initial phases, followed by iterative model building and crystallographic refinement (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the methodology used for structure determination.

claim: The structure of uncomplexed CyRPA was determined by molecular replacement using the CyRPA component of the Fab-complexed structure as a search model.
source: Crystals were also obtained of uncomplexed CyRPA; this structure was determined by molecular replacement, using the CyRPA component of the Fab-complexed structure as a search model, and subsequently refined using diffraction data to 3.09 Å resolution.
evidence: This describes the methodology used for structure determination.

claim: CyRPA displays the canonical six-bladed β-propeller (6BBP) fold.
source: The CyRPA structure (Figure 3) displays the canonical six-bladed β-propeller (6BBP) fold (Figure 3A and B) (Chen et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3 and cited reference (Chen et al., 2011b).

claim: Within the β-propeller structure are four intra-sheet disulfide bonds (Cys19-Cys35, Cys90-Cys92, Cys151-Cys169 and Cys229-Cys239) and one inter-sheet disulfide bond (Cys274-Cys298).
source: Within the β-propeller structure are four intra-sheet disulfide bonds (Cys19-Cys35, Cys90-Cys92, Cys151-Cys169 and Cys229-Cys239) and one inter-sheet disulfide bond (Cys274-Cys298) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3.

claim: The crystal of uncomplexed CyRPA contains four copies of the protein in the crystallographic asymmetric unit, arranged with approximate 222-point group symmetry.
source: The crystal of uncomplexed CyRPA contains four copies of the protein in the crystallographic asymmetric unit, arranged with approximate 222-point group symmetry (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The monomer-monomer interfaces are most likely an artefact of crystallization.
source: The monomer-monomer interfaces, although extensive, are most likely an artefact of crystallization, as we find no evidence for higher-order association upon SEC of CyRPA.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of evidence for higher-order association in SEC experiments.

claim: The closest structural homologue to CyRPA is the attachment glycoprotein of a henipah virus isolated from Ghanaian bats (PDB entry 4UF7).
source: A DALI search (Holm and Rosenstrom, 2010) reveals that the closest structural homologue to CyRPA is the attachment glycoprotein of a henipah virus isolated from Ghanaian bats (PDB entry 4UF7 (Lee et al., 2015)), with the next closest homologues being various sialidases of viral, bacterial and mammalian origin (Varghese et al., 1983; Newstead et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on a DALI search and supported by citations (Holm and Rosenstrom, 2010; Lee et al., 2015).

claim: CyRPA has up to 16% sequence identity with all structural homologues found by the DALI search.
source: CyRPA has up to 16% sequence identity with all such structural homologues found by the DALI search, suggesting only distant evolutionary relationships, if any, with other thus-far structurally-characterized 6BBPs.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: No significant sialidase activity was detected for recombinant CyRPA.
source: We further tested whether the recombinant CyRPA had sialidase activity, using the fluorogenic substrate 4-methylumbelliferyl N-acetyl-α-D-neuraminic acid as a substrate (see Methods), with bacterial sialidase (neuraminidase) from Arthrobacter ureafaciens as a positive control (Saito et al., 1979). No significant sialidase activity was detected (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CyRPA is not a functional sialidase.
source: We thus conclude that CyRPA is not a functional sialidase.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the lack of conserved sialidase motifs and the absence of sialidase activity in experimental assays.

claim: The Fab fragment of 8A7 binds to the region of CyRPA comprising residues from the loop between the second and third strands of the first β-sheet (Gly41, Glu42 and Glu45), residues from the loop between the first and second β-sheets (Asp63, Lys66, Glu67, Thr68, Asp69, Leu70 and Thr71), residues from the loop between the second and third strands of the second β-sheet (Lys91 and Lys99), and residues comprising the N-terminal region of the fourth strand of the second β-sheet (Asn116, Asn117, Ala118 and Glu119).
source: The Fab fragment of 8A7 Figure 3B binds to the region of CyRPA comprising residues from the loop between the second and third strands of the first β-sheet (Gly41, Glu42 and Glu45), residues from the loop between the first and second β-sheets (Asp63, Lys66, Glu67, Thr68, Asp69, Leu70 and Thr71), residues from the loop between the second and third strands of the second β-sheet (Lys91 and Lys99), and residues comprising the N-terminal region of the fourth strand of the second β-sheet (Asn116, Asn117, Ala118 and Glu119) (Figure 3B, Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure of the CyRPA/Fab complex shown in Figure 4.

claim: Comparison with the uncomplexed CyRPA structures reveals only minor changes in rotameric conformation and relative disposition of CyRPA residues at the interface.
source: Comparison with the uncomplexed CyRPA structures reveals only minor changes in rotameric conformation and relative disposition of CyRPA residues at the interface.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison of the complexed and uncomplexed CyRPA structures.

claim: The antigen interaction involves residues drawn from all six complementary-determining regions (CDRs) of the Fab and buries a total of 1634 Å of the molecular surface across both molecules.
source: The antigen interaction involves residues drawn from all six complementary-determining regions (CDRs) of the Fab and buries a total of 1634 Å of the molecular surface across both molecules (Figure 4A,B and C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4.

claim: The shape complementarity of the interface (Sc = 0.71) is relatively high for antibody-antigen complexes.
source: The shape complementarity of the interface (Sc = 0.71) is relatively high for antibody-antigen complexes (Lawrence and Colman, 1993), with the surface of CyRPA epitope being predominantly negatively charged (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with known antibody-antigen complexes (Lawrence and Colman, 1993).

claim: The interface involves a rich network of approximately nineteen hydrogen bonds.
source: The interface itself involves a rich network of approximately nineteen hydrogen bonds (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The closest structural homologue to CyRPA is the attachment glycoprotein of a henipah virus which binds to ephrinB2 and is important for host cell entry.
source: The closest structural homologue to CyRPA is the attachment glycoprotein of a henipah virus which binds to ephrinB2 and is important for host cell entry (Lee et al., 2015); however, it also has some similarity to bacterial and viral sialidases all of which have a six-bladed β-propeller fold (Varghese et al., 1983; Crennell et al., 1996, 1993, 1994).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and supported by citations (Lee et al., 2015; Varghese et al., 1983; Crennell et al., 1996, 1993, 1994).

claim: The PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex functions together as conditional expression of CyRPA or PfRipr and blocking of PfRh5 binding to basigin blocks merozoite invasion at the same step.
source: The PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex functions together as a conditional expression of CyRPA or PfRipr and blocking of PfRh5 binding to basigin blocks merozoite invasion at the same step (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Volz et al., 2016.

claim: Merozoites lacking PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex function can still interact and deform the erythrocyte membrane but they cannot form the pore or discontinuity between the parasite apical end and the erythrocyte membrane through which Ca2+ passes.
source: Merozoites lacking PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex function can still interact and deform the erythrocyte membrane but they cannot form the pore or discontinuity between the parasite apical end and the erythrocyte membrane through which Ca2+ passes (Volz et al., 2016; Weiss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Volz et al., 2016 and Weiss et al., 2015.

claim: Merozoites lacking PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex function do not progress to form a tight junction which requires insertion of the RON complex into the host cell.
source: Therefore, they do not progress to form a tight junction which requires insertion of the RON complex into the host cell (Weiss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weiss et al., 2015.

claim: The PfRh5 structure has a large coiled-coil domain that has some structural similarity with the N-terminal coiled-coil domain of SipB and other similar proteins.
source: The PfRh5 structure has a large coiled-coil domain that has some structural similarity with the N-terminal coiled-coil domain of SipB and other similar proteins (Barta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Barta et al., 2012.

claim: SipB forms part of the Salmonella type III secretion system that transports effector proteins across the host cell membrane.
source: SipB forms part of the Salmonella type III secretion system that transports effector proteins across the host cell membrane.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about bacterial secretion systems.

claim: There are six-bladed β–propeller structured proteins, similar to CyRPA, that play a role in the formation of protein translocation channels by bacterial pathogens to inject virulence factors.
source: Additionally, there are six-bladed β–propeller structured proteins, similar to CyRPA, that play a role in the formation of protein translocation channels by bacterial pathogens to inject virulence factors (Meusch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Meusch et al., 2014.

claim: The link between the formation of a pore between the merozoite surface and the erythrocyte membrane by the PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr is circumstantial and requires further evidence.
source: Whilst these similarities are tantalizing, the link between the formation of a pore between the merozoite surface and the erythrocyte membrane by the PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr is circumstantial and requires further evidence (Volz et al., 2016; Weiss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging the need for more evidence, supported by citations (Volz et al., 2016; Weiss et al., 2015).

claim: CyRPA binds to PfRh5 in the PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr tripartite complex.
source: Our experiments show that CyRPA binds to PfRh5 in the PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr tripartite complex and it is likely that it also interacts directly with PfRipr (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: It is likely that CyRPA also interacts directly with PfRipr.
source: Our experiments show that CyRPA binds to PfRh5 in the PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr tripartite complex and it is likely that it also interacts directly with PfRipr (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the tripartite complex formation, supported by citation (Volz et al., 2016).

claim: The tripartite complex only forms at the interface between the apical end of the merozoite and the erythrocyte membrane.
source: The subcellular localization of CyRPA and PfRipr is in the micronemes whereas PfRh5 is at the neck of the rhoptries and the tripartite complex only forms at the interface between the apical end of the merozoite and the erythrocyte membrane.
evidence: This is based on prior work cited in the manuscript (Volz et al., 2016).

claim: All three proteins (PfRh5, CyRPA, PfRipr) are spread over the free merozoite surface but generally CyRPA and PfRipr co-localise whereas PfRh5 does not.
source: All three proteins are spread over the free merozoite surface but generally CyRPA and PfRipr co-localise whereas PfRh5 does not.
evidence: This is based on prior work cited in the manuscript (Volz et al., 2016).

claim: The PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex forms during the invasion process when it is required and its assembly is finely regulated, most likely requiring the function of other unknown proteins.
source: This suggests that the PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex forms during the invasion process when it is required and that its assembly is finely regulated, most likely requiring the function of other unknown proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the localization data.

claim: It is not understood how the PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex or CyRPA associates with the merozoite membrane as none of these proteins have a transmembrane domain or a GPI anchor.
source: It is also not understood how the PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex or CyRPA associates with the merozoite membrane as none of these proteins have a transmembrane domain or a GPI anchor (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in understanding, supported by citation (Volz et al., 2016).

claim: The anti-CyRPA monoclonal antibody 8A7 directly abrogates the interaction of CyRPA with PfRh5 and as a result directly blocks merozoite invasion of P. falciparum into human erythrocytes.
source: The anti-CyRPA monoclonal antibody 8A7 directly abrogates the interaction of CyRPA with PfRh5 and as a result directly blocks merozoite invasion of P. falciparum into human erythrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2C.

claim: The PfRh5 binding site for CyRPA overlaps with (or lies close to) the antibody conformational epitope.
source: This suggests that the PfRh5 binding site for CyRPA overlaps with (or lies close to) the antibody conformational epitope, defined by residues within the loop between the second and third strands of the first β-sheet, the loop between the first and second β-sheets, and residues at the N-terminus region of the fourth strand of the second β-sheet.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of the antibody to block CyRPA-PfRh5 interaction.

claim: The absence of large conformational change within CyRPA upon Fab complexation rules out an allosteric mechanism of abrogating a complex formation with PfRh5.
source: The absence of large conformational change within CyRPA upon Fab complexation rules out an allosteric mechanism of abrogating a complex formation with PfRh5.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison of complexed and uncomplexed CyRPA.

claim: Blocking of the CyRPA and PfRh5 interaction by antibodies is consistent with a functional PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex assembling at the interface between the invading merozoite and erythrocyte membrane.
source: Therefore, blocking of the CyRPA and PfRh5 interaction by antibodies is consistent with a functional PfRh5/CyRPA/PfRipr complex assembling at the interface between the invading merozoite and erythrocyte membrane (Volz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citation (Volz et al., 2016).

claim: CyRPA is a highly conserved protein in P. falciparum.
source: CyRPA is a highly conserved protein in P. falciparum and the antibody binding epitope as well as the remainder of the protein is not under selective pressure.
evidence: This represents knowledge about the conservation of CyRPA in P. falciparum populations.

claim: The antibody binding epitope of CyRPA as well as the remainder of the protein is not under selective pressure.
source: CyRPA is a highly conserved protein in P. falciparum and the antibody binding epitope as well as the remainder of the protein is not under selective pressure.
evidence: This represents knowledge about the conservation of CyRPA in P. falciparum populations.

claim: CyRPA is a promising vaccine candidate as antibodies inhibit merozoite invasion in vitro as well as in mice engrafted with human erythrocytes.
source: As a result, it is a promising vaccine candidate as antibodies inhibit merozoite invasion in vitro as well as in mice engrafted with human erythrocytes (Reddy et al., 2014; Dreyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Reddy et al., 2014; Dreyer et al., 2012) and the data presented in this manuscript.
